speechtext:
I thank the committee for
giving me the opportunity of making a few further observations.
This situation in Berlin, which is the immediate problem confronting the nations of the world, is characteristic of the times in which we live. No sooner had the trouble in the Middle East been dampened last year than this was followed by fires in the Far East. Then when the conflagration in the Formosa straits was dying out the problem of Berlin and Germany arose.
This, of course, is the pattern of our times. Soviet union dexterity brings us from one crisis to another in rapid fire succession. However, we have an interest in this problem altogether apart from the fact that, as a nation among the nations of the world, we are interested in the preservation of good relations among states.
[Mr Martin (Essex East).]

Our interest in the Berlin situation has not only this wide political interest. It has as well a juridical or legal basis. First of all, we will all recall that it was in November last that the premier of the Soviet union indicated that the time had come for the western powers to leave Berlin; and on November 27 last he proposed the western withdrawal from West Berlin and the creation of a demilitarized free city. It will also be recalled that he had indicated that a settlement must be reached by May 27. That position was later modified, perhaps as a result of the intervention of Mr. Macmillan who, we all agree, took a wise course in going to Moscow, as he did, in order to make a fact-finding assessment of the Russian position.
But I say that our interest in this problem has a juridical basis as well as arising out of our existence as a sovereign state. It will be recalled that the three powers met in London on October 2, 1954, when they conferred to lay plans for the termination of the occupation of the Federal Republic of Germany and for the incorporation of that state into NATO. It was at this conference that they made this declaration:
The security and welfare of Berlin and the maintenance of the position of the three powers there are regarded by the three powers as essential elements to the peace of the free world in the present international situation. Accordingly, they will maintain armed forces within the territory of Berlin as long as their responsibilities require it. They therefore reaffirm that they will treat any attack against Berlin from any quarter as an attack upon their forces and themselves.
Canada along with other NATO powers on October 23, 1954 associated itself with this declaration. That Canada as well as the United States and other NATO powers have a stake in the problem of Germany and Berlin flows from this association with this declaration, and also from the obligation incurred under article 6 of the North Atlantic treaty under which an armed attack on the occupation forces in Europe of any party to the treaty constitutes an attack on all parties.
As I indicated a while ago, we approved the decision of the British Prime Minister to go to Moscow, and in so doing I take it that we wanted to assert that initiative of that kind could not be looked upon as an appeasing act. It was doing something which British leaders have done from the time of William Pitt when they have sought to deal with hostile foreign powers. This visit of Mr. Macmillan and further interventions of this sort need not be regarded as appeasement. They mean no more than what they have meant in the past. Certainly this visit on the part of the British Prime Minister did not

mean that the United Kingdom likes Mr. Khrushchev's communist imperialism any more than Englishmen liked Napoleon Bonaparte's revolutionary imperialism. I believe that association or intercourse with those who do not share our ideological objectives is all to the good, and that it is only by conference leading ultimately to adjudication and, let us hope, even conciliation that we can find, in the absence of war, a solution to these vital issues which affect us more than anything else either on the international or the domestic front.
We must not overlook the dangers in the situation. It must not be forgotten that Mr. Khrushchev in his note-I think some time in the month of February-to this government said that any attempt by the western powers to maintain access to West Berlin by force will be opposed by force and will lead to war. These statements must be assessed in the full context of the situation that confront us and in which they have been made. But I think all of us in this chamber will support the attitude taken by the government, certainly in the statement made by my hon. friend's predecessor, that we believe that negotiation even in this extremely difficult matter can lead to settlement.
I for one welcomed the statement made by the Minister of National Defence, when, speaking at the anniversary meeting of NATO, he indicated a possible ultimate role in this situation for the United Nations. This suggestion of a potential role for the United Nations had been referred to in this house in an earlier speech by my leader. It had been referred to, as my hon. friend will recall, much earlier by Mr. Khrushchev and by Mr. Macmillan. The Minister of National Defence, if I properly read his words as delivered in Washington, had suggested a method by which the United Nations might provide a framework for any four power agreement on Berlin. He saw that the basic role of the United Nations might be to verify that all parties were abiding by the terms of the agreement, the essential part of which would be a Soviet pledge by binding itself and its associates to permit full freedom of access to West Berlin and the acceptance of the United Nations presence on the lines of communication.
There are good precedents for the suggestion made by Canada, a suggestion that 1 hope will be followed up by the Canadian government if whatever kind of settlement is reached lends itself to such further persistency of suggestion. As I say, there are precedents for the use of the United Nations in this kind of role. There is, of course, no complete parallel between many other instrumentalities of the United Nations in this
Supply

External Affairs particular situation, but there are similar features of principle that I think serve as a precedent.
The para-military body, the United Nations emergency force with which the Leader of the Opposition, to the everlasting gratitude of the people of the world, had so much to do, is in itself in principle an indication at least of the potential role which in a situation such as that in West Berlin the United Nations might ultimately play. The work of the United Nations observation group in Lebanon is another example of the use of the United Nations in matters that have to do with conflicts either between groups within the same nation or between one nation and another. Certainly the work of the international supervisory organization under General Van Horne operating between Jordan, the United Arab Republic and Israel is an indication of the growing awareness of the usefulness of the United Nations in these situations. Perhaps the most effective and the closest parallel, however, was the formula devised by the secretary general of the United Nations last year when he suggested the idea of a United Nations presence located in the capital of Jordan, as a means to maintain tranquility, which has lasted even longer than its most ardent sponsors at the time thought possible.
So I trust the Canadian government in its studies of the Berlin situation and in the recommendations it will make during the discussions it will have with the Secretary of State of the United States will bear in mind the successful previous usages of the United Nations instrumentality, and will seek to impress upon freedom-loving nations the desirability of noting that in the charter of the United Nations are to be found many of the methods by which some solutions can be made easier and more lasting. I hope that in the matter of Berlin, Canada is using her best offices to make her concern felt and to indicate the result of her consideration as to ways and means by which solutions can be found which will lead to an easing of international tensions and not add to the turbulence which prevails in the world at the present time.
The hon. gentleman covered a wide area, and I naturally do not propose to attempt to do the same, except to say that he will find in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization the same opportunity for constructive statesmanship as I believe he will find at the United Nations. Canada has, of course, the greatest interest in this organization. It was one of our former prime ministers who first in the United Nations gave expression, in 1947, to
5724	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-External Affairs the desirability of a defensive alliance of freedom-loving states within the terms of article 51 of the United Nations charter. It was a Canadian government backed by public opinion in Canada that caused demands to be made to expand the purposes and the functions of this organization.
But the hon. gentleman will perhaps want to remember carefully the words which were uttered by the Leader of the Opposition when he spoke on April 14, 1959 taking as his subject "Ten years of NATO", and concluded what he had to say with these words:
The Atlantic nations are now facing a supreme test of their capacity to unite. If they fail in this, they may find it difficult to prosper and even survive as free nations. This test is the inescapable result of the tragic experiences of the recent past. Success in meeting it is made the more essential by the awful necessities of a thermonuclear future. Can we combine our national strengths, merge our national policies, and submerge our national prejudices to meet this test? If we cannot-or do not-then far more than NATO may be lost in the next ten years.
He was thinking not only of the failure to live up to the terms of article 2; he was thinking not only of the fact that the studies of three foreign ministers in the NATO group had not been implemented. He was thinking too of the stresses and strains that are being placed on this defensive alliance by the unfolding events of our time. Canada is not only a member of NATO; she is a member of that important triangular group of western nations which includes the United States and Great Britain. She is also a member of the commonwealth and as well, a member of the United Nations; and while she will wish in the interests of her own security to preserve the unity of NATO and to preserve the unity of this group of three nations, she will want at the same time to make a contribution to a wider unity, the unity of the world; and the opportunity for doing that will arise at the United Nations.
Not only is our external policy reflected in policy itself, but it is reflected in the permanent personnel of the Department of External Affairs. We can accept the judgment of those outside this country who speak of our public servants in this department in the highest praise. It is, of course, necessary to do everything possible to maintain the morale of those who are employed in this department and, of course, the organization within the department is a matter which the minister may want to look into carefully from time to time. He may want to examine, for example, whether or not the process of rotation of personnel is too rapid, particularly in the light of the loss of certain personnel in recent months. He may want to examine whether or not this acceleration in the process [Mr Martin (Essex East).]
of rotation has resulted in giving to personalities involved less opportunity for acquiring specialized knowledge in certain divisions of the department than they would otherwise have had.
I simply ask the minister to give consideration as to whether or not recent developments do not suggest that quicker rotation of personnel in the department may have resulted in less opportunity for the acquisition of specialized knowledge in certain divisions than we should like to see for instance in the trade division, the Middle East division, the United States-Canada division and, I should think too, the legal division. In any event the minister will find many things to do as he now takes on, free from other obligations, these responsibilities as the spokesman and chief formulator of government foreign policy.
The minister may be convinced, as I said at the beginning, of one thing. He will have the good will of every member of this house, as he has the good will, I am sure, of the great majority of the people of Canada. In this field of international affairs our differences are limited. This does not mean to say that there will not be occasions when we shall find it necessary to take strong issue with him; but as the Prime Minister indicated in his speech before the general assembly in September of 1957, the basic lines of Canadian foreign policy are observed by this as by previous governments.
We are living at a very difficult time. We have not the answer to many of the problems which confront us. We want to see our society remain free; we want to see the democratic way of life persist. We have to take into account the exigencies and the problems which confront us. We have a responsibility, regardless of power and position, to play a full and continuing role in the solution of the great issues which divide mankind.
There is a Canadian point of view. That point of view has been ably and vigorously expressed in the past. The minister's success in this portfolio will depend on his seizing the opportunity that is now his in the face of difficult situations, putting forward the considered judgment of the government of which he is a member, in the hope that an objective approach in these matters will be capable of preserving existing desirable unities and at the same time laying the foundations for a world that will be ruled by law and not by brute force.
In this connection the minister, I hope, will give consideration to what may be done about making the international court of justice a more effective instrument than I believe it is at the present time. In my judgment it is not the effective instrument

it was intended to be. It is certainly not as strong as the international court of justice created under the covenant. The United States now has taken an initiative in this matter. The vice president of the United States, and the President have said that the government of the United States is prepared to give consideration to the elimination of the optional clause and to recognizing the compulsory jurisdiction of the court. I would think that Canada, in spite of the difficulties arising because of the constitution of the court and because of the difficulties involved in matters of domestic jurisdiction under article 2(7) of the charter of the United Nations could, like the United States, give a lead in this matter.
The peace of the world is the most important consideration before all of us. That being the case the policy of the government of Canada in its relations with other states is the most important of any of the responsibilities of government. It is because of the tremendous responsibility involved that I sincerely trust that the minister will understand the spirit in which I have expressed some criticism and given some indication of my confidence that he approaches his task only with the desire to continue seeing to it that Canada makes worthy contributions to the preservation of peace.
Our contributions are not made for the purpose of increasing our prestige, but prestige and worthy contributions can go side by side. The result will be enhancement for this nation as well as the realization of a contribution made toward the solution of the great problem of our time, the preservation of peace among the nations.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SIGNING OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened this morning very attentively to the comprehensive speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I intend to comment upon it later at various points in my remarks. I must explain, however, that I am going to do something this afternoon that I very much dislike doing, and that is rely on extensive notes. The reason I do this is that I want to have the opportunity in the time permitted me to deal with a number of subjects in this very important and wide field, and at the same time present the policy of this group on several aspects of external affairs.
The minister has assumed office, as was stated by the previous speaker, with the good will and best wishes of all hon. members of this committee, at a most critical and interesting time in international and Canadian affairs. I say that because we are on a balanced wheel where so little could mean
Supply-External Affairs so much in either direction. I would term this the period of the hush before the dawn or, if we fail to act with common sense, before the gloom.
Let me assure the minister before I proceed with my remarks that in this debate and on this question we seek no party advantage in this group but advance our policies, ideas, suggestions and opinions as a contribution to the common pool of our thought in an effort to do our part in establishing and maintaining world peace and stability.
I was very interested to note that the minister observed that Canadians are interested in foreign affairs and in the part that Canada will play toward developing world co-operation, or words to that effect. How true. I think Canadians generally are becoming more and more interested in foreign affairs because of their realization of the vital importance of the decisions that have to be made in certain fields in the near future by the major nations.
I noticed that shortly after that the minister invited suggestions and opinions. I was pleased to hear him do that, because as I said previously the minister enters office with the good will and best wishes of all hon. members of this committee. But as the hon. member who has just taken his seat said, when speaking for the official opposition- I always have to be so careful when I deal with them. You know, they are a little jealous of this little group at this end; they want to re-emphasize their importance. But I think I got it right that time. We will no doubt differ with respect to policies put forward in certain fields, but whether we agree or differ we are giving our honest opinions and putting forward honest suggestions and ideas as the result of thought on both sides of the committee, to the end that we seek a common objective and common goal.
During recent months Canada in our opinion has lost some of its former and close contacts in the field of international affairs, and unfortunately, to some extent, because of the death of the minister's predecessor which we all regret. We all miss him at this time. But this lapse in having an active secretary of state for external affairs has caused some loss of contact with the United Nations and with other capitals of the world. This will give the minister a somewhat strenuous time in the months ahead in his attempts to overcome the handicap in this regard under which he starts his new duties.
In supporting that point of view I want to quote an editorial from the Globe and Mail of Thursday, May 14, 1959 entitled "Defence and Sovereignty" to indicate the need for Canada to speak with a stronger voice and resume its former close contacts with the

Supply-External Affairs United Nations and with various countries and capitals of the world. This is what this editorial has to say:
Today, as never before, the world's eyes are upon Canada. In part, this is because of her progress and prosperity; in part, because of the reputation she has gained as a free and fair-minded middle power, respected by most nations, feared by none.
I want to pause at this stage to pay a tribute to the present Leader of the Opposition, who was for a long time secretary of state for external affairs. There is no question but that hon. gentleman made a great contribution toward the maintenance of world peace and recognition of Canada's status abroad. I continue:
From this, Canadians may take satisfaction. But there is another, more subtle reason why the world watches Canada; it judges us in order to judge the United States.
The world sees Canada working very closely with the United States. It measures the integrity of the United States by the extent to which Canada, in this situation, retains her own integrity. Assuming the United States wishes to keep and strengthen its position as leader of the western nations, it must govern its relationship with Canada so that Canada not only is, but gives every evidence of being, independent.
This is essential to Canada's world status, as well. If we wish to keep and strengthen our own unique position among the nations, we must constantly demonstrate our political sovereignty, our economic sovereignty-
This is the task that faces the new minister at the present time. This has been the spearhead, as it were, of this most important department for some months.
Then the Globe and Mail again, of Saturday, May 16 of this year:
It is just as essential to Ottawa's international status as it is to Washington's that Canada should not only be, but in all matters should appear to be, fully autonomous. To become a much respected middle power, this country had to gain its independence from Britain. To stay a much respected middle power, we must regain our independence from the United States.
This is an editorial in a paper that generally supports the party in power.
In our opinion the minister will require to spend considerable time at the United Nations, in the various capitals of the world and in other places in order to restore the personal contact which is so important for a person in his office. I might say, Mr. Chairman, he has to take advantage of every opportunity to win and influence friends. I will say this before leaving the subject. If the minister is as successful in the international field in winning and influencing friends as he has been in this house in the last 22 years, then our foreign policy will proceed with great success.
There is no necessity to speak at length with respect to the meetings of the standing committee on external affairs, Mr. Chairman


The committee held 10 meetings and dealt very thoroughly in detail with the estimates of the department. I must say at this time that the meetings of the committee and its proceedings were necessarily restricted and pervaded with a great sense of loss by the untimely death of the former secretary of state for external affairs, Dr. Sidney E. Smith. I should also say at this time how much the committee regretted the passing of Mr. W. D. Matthews, the assistant under secretary of state for external affairs, both of whom the committee in its deliberations found of great assistance.
I might say a word or two about the personnel of the department. You get a good idea of the quality of the staff of a department, Mr. Chairman, when you have had experience on a committee over a number of years, when the members of that staff representing its various branches come before the committee to give their explanations with respect to expenditures and forms of administration, give the reasons for this and that. I might say in passing that the minister himself has not been at all backward in digging into these matters during years past as a member of the standing committee on external affairs. As I said before, we get a good idea of the quality of the staff. There is no question about it, in my opinion after a number of years' experience on this committee, but that Canada is very fortunate in the quality of the staff who are administering the Department of External Affairs.
I will have some reference to make to the minister's remarks later, but I wish to take this opportunity to advance the views of this group on this important subject in several aspects. From this point on I shall be dealing with the C.C.F. policy with respect to certain aspects of foreign affairs. Naturally I can only cover the major points in which we are interested. No doubt there will be some other aspects of foreign affairs on which our point of view will be covered by other members of this group later on in this debate.
First we believe that Canada should maintain an independent, co-operative and constructive foreign policy of her own. We ought not, as has been too often the case in the past, simply to reflect the views of our southern neighbour, the United States. Certainly we in the C.C.F. are prepared, as I believe all Canadians are prepared, to work in close co-operation with the United States. We ought to make it perfectly clear that we have a mind of our own and certain ideas of our own which we think can he constructive international councils. We believe that the Canadian representatives at the United Nations ought to speak up more vigorously than often has been the case in the past for

constructive approaches to all these problems, even though those approaches may not always be appreciated by our United States friends.
Second, the fundamental tenet of our approach to international affairs is that we must expand and encourage the development of the United Nations. We know that the United Nations has had many failures, but we believe, too, that there are undreamed of possibilities for promoting international peace through the agencies of the United Nations, the constructive work of which is not recognized in many quarters. We hope, for example, that if the specific tensions can be eased the United Nations can eventually develop a world police force which will be responsible for maintaining the peace in critical areas. We have given a good lead in that direction with respect to the Middle East in the way of observer corps and things of that sort. We of this group hope that will be the development with respect to military forces of the future, used finally, we hope, purely to police the unruly people of the world.
We believe that the United Nations offers tremendous possibilities as a focus in channelling economic aid. Indeed, we dare to hope that one day the United Nations may become an effective world government, although we recognize that is some distance in the future. Perhaps these things seem visionary in a world of conflict such as ours. If we are to have a permanent and lasting peace, we in this group firmly believe that we must move consciously in those directions.
A third and an important point in our basic policy is that at all times we must be prepared to sit down and negotiate outstanding issues. Sabre rattling solves nothing; still less will atomic war solve anything. I was very pleased, in listening to the minister's remarks this morning, to hear his comments with respect to the need for patience and continued negotiations. I like his mood, his attitude and his frame of mind in that respect. It was interesting to hear the minister say that war is unthinkable. Apparently all of us in this house agree on these basic points at this time. What is required is a convinced determination to negotiate specific issues, such as Germany, in the hope that by solving one aspect of the problem trust will be engendered for tackling other aspects. The minister in talking about this problem of patience and negotiation, mentioned the hope that the summit meeting would be resumed and that all those meetings tend to work for a reduction of world tensions. I liked that very much indeed in his approach to these negotiations.
My fourth basic point, and undoubtedly the most important of all, is this. We in this
Supply-External Affairs group believe that the future of the western world as we know it, and indeed the future of the world itself, will hinge not so much on military might but on what we do to promote the economic and democratic development of those nations in the world which have come to be known as underdeveloped. Not only must we develop trade policies which will enable the western nations to compete with the Soviet union, but we must develop a much bolder and more imaginative policy with respect to promoting economic development in other areas of the world.
Now here is perhaps the most crucial point in the whole approach of the C.C.F. to the question of international affairs. We in the C.C.F. are democratic socialists, and if this party ever fails to be socialist I say right now that I shall be out of it, and quickly. We reject communism and the theories of communism. But we know too that our system of economics, known as capitalism, is also incompetent to deal with basic world problems.
Look at some of the contradictions that we have in the world today. You cannot blame them on individuals. They are the result of world revolution, historical development and so on. How can we expect the development of oil in the Middle East in the interests of the Arab people when we tolerate its exploitation by a few giant monopolies? How can we promote economic development throughout the world if we are prepared to tolerate an economy at home which operates away below capacity and during certain periods tolerates large scale unemployment? How can we expect people in other parts of the world to understand and believe in our democracy if we have great surpluses of food while there are people starving in other parts of the world? I am confident that by accepting our responsibilities in all these fields we will not only be helping these people of whom I have been speaking but we will be helping ourselves.
In that respect the committee on external affairs studied some aspects of international aid, particularly the Colombo plan, technical assistance and the refugee problem. I was very glad to hear the minister mention increased assistance to commonwealth countries under the Colombo plan and technical and similar assistance to the other countries he mentioned. These are continued steps in the right direction and I judge that the government, before making this decision, read the final report of the committee on external affairs because in that report the interest of the committee in this most important question is clearly indicated. We in this group simply say; Take every advantage of, shall I say, our favoured position in the world

Supply-External Affairs today to do more and more to assist these underdeveloped countries and in doing so assist ourselves.
We in the C.C.F. group urge the government to take advantage of every opportunity to strengthen the ties within the commonwealth and in doing so strengthen the spokes of this great balance wheel in international affairs. When the minister was speaking on the question of the commonwealth this morning I noticed that he said: "The commonwealth is foremost in our minds; it is a beneficial influence on the affairs of mankind." If that is the minister's opinion, and I know it is, we in this group stand together with the minister on his approach to developing closer ties within the commonwealth and strengthening the commonwealth because of its influence on the affairs of mankind. We wish him well in all he does in that respect.
I want to say a few words about European affairs, and I refer to western Europe. You know, Mr. Chairman, I have had the feeling at times when I glance up to the right that there are some pained expressions on some of the gentlemen's faces but I hope they will bear with me a little longer. In our opinion, first consideration should be given to a plan whereby troops would be withdrawn from an area in central Europe. This area should include not only East and West Germany but Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary as well. In brief, we believe there are great possibilities in what is known as the Rapacki plan and that its possibilities should be explored more and more in the days ahead. We believe there should be a belt through the centre of Europe which could be neutralized and demilitarized. We believe that this sort of neutral belt running through what we term the crisis area of Europe would make a real contribution toward the easing of tension in that important part of the world.
Our second proposal is that the western powers should be prepared to consider the creation of a loose federation of the governments of East and West Germany as a first step toward the holding of free elections throughout all Germany. In our opinion this could be a step toward breaking the deadlock which has been created by the west's insistence on free elections as a first step and the Russian determination to resist free elections. We offer these suggestions, Mr. Chairman, after much consideration of this very serious and delicate problem.
As I have said, we welcome the indications of a more flexible attitude on the part of both the west and the Soviet union. Regardless of, shall I say, the hubbub that has gone on, I think we must welcome the fact that the talks have continued and that there has been


even a minor degree of give and take on both sides, which I think is a hopeful state of affairs from which to view the future. We believe that the western powers could be still more vigorous in making specific proposals. It is through our grasping the initiative that there is the best possibility of our being in a strong position when we come to the negotiating table.
Here I wish to refer to the tribute the minister paid to the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Right Hon. Mr. Macmillan. We want to join in that tribute. I think that in the recent negotiations and developments with respect to East and West Germany and western Europe he has given a most stable and commendable lead and has shown exceptional balance which has had a tremendous influence on the discussions at Geneva concerning this difficult problem. This is indicated, I think by the difference in attitude toward this conference between the Prime Minister of Great Britain and the secretary of state of the United States in their published comments with respect to the success or lack of success, whichever viewpoint they took, in connection with this most important conference of foreign ministers in Geneva. In that connection I want to read briefly from an editorial in the Globe and Mail of Friday, July 3. It is entitled, "Fruits of Negotiation", and quotes Mr. Macmillan as follows:
I feel this prize is worth waiting and working for, because it is the biggest of all.
I think these are very wise words indeed. It is easy enough to show impatience and have quick cuts to success and quick remedies for the disease of world instability, but I think those are very wise words indeed. "I feel this prize is worth waiting and working for, because it is the biggest of all."
I want to say a few words with respect to China. I have listened with interest to what the minister had to say. I understand that there is no change in the government's policy with respect to China since the statement made earlier this session by Dr. Sidney Smith. We fully appreciate the difficulties mentioned by the minister. I must say that the government of China does not make it any easier for the government to consider recognition. We quite understand that, particularly in view of the recent happenings in Tibet. But we who come from British Columbia realize that we now have a minister who comes from British Columbia and no doubt on that account he fully appreciates the opinion of a great number of important people in that province in industry, labour and agriculture with respect to the need for recognition of China.
Our policy in favour of the recognition of the communist government of China has

always been very clear. We believe now that the soundness of our position in this regard is all the more obvious. Many prominent Canadians, including industrial leaders and bankers, have visited China and all have come back with the conviction that the recognition of China and her admittance into the United Nations would be in the interests of world peace.
To us the case for recognizing Red China has always seemed an obvious one. No one, to our knowledge, has ever argued that recognition implies agreement with a government's policy. It simply means recognition of the existence of the effective government of that country and willingness to live together in the same world.
We must all realize that China is a developing industrial power-we are getting more evidence of that day after day-and that she is going to be a force in future world politics whether or not we like it. Surely it makes sense for us to recognize her and extend our trade with her, and to be prepared to discuss with her, through the United Nations, the issues over which she will have increasing influence. There is no doubt that that influence is going to increase.
Before leaving this topic we do urge the minister to give further consideration to this problem of the recognition of China, in the interests of world peace as a whole, in the interests of Canadians generally, and particularly in the interest of the province from which the minister comes.
I want now to refer to another vitally important area of the world, the Middle East. I am hurrying along because of the time and the vastness of this subject. During the last century the policies of the western nations in the Middle East cannot have been said to have been very honourable, and I think that is an understatement. We have dealt with the whole area in typical imperialist fashion. We cannot blame certain individuals for a particular period in history. We have allowed giant private oil monopolies to exploit the region and make tremendous profits at the expense of the local inhabitants. They continue to do this and to control and dominate their governments. This control by oil companies is the seed of all the unrest in the Middle East, and any form of democratic expression is virtually impossible. The policies of the Soviet union in the area in recent years have been no better. They have looked upon the countries of the Middle East as pawns in their game of international power politics. The unfortunate thing is that we in the west have responded on a number of occasions in much the same fashion.
This is a question beyond the capacity of Canada to solve. It is a very wide question
Supply

External Affairs which will only be solved as the result of the development of the lessening of tensions and a more constructive view of international problems on the part of a good many nations in the world. We in the C.C.F. advance the suggestion I am going to make as one end to which we could work, and we are convinced that as long as oil reserves and the vast natural resources of the Middle East remain in the hands of a few giant monopolies in western countries we will not have settled peace in the Middle East, and the people of those countries will not have the standard of living they are entitled to with the resources they enjoy. We believe that it is time to take a bold and courageously new approach to the Middle Eastern situation.
The key to our proposal is this, that the Arab people should be assisted, through the United Nations, to take over for themselves the ownership and control of their oil resources. I realize that the minister will say that that is a big order and cannot be done overnight. But it can be done little by little, giving these people a larger share of the wealth which is being exported from their country at the present time. We believe that through the good offices of the United Nations this could be done in a peaceful and orderly way over a period of time. The best method might be the establishment of an international Middle East development commission, which would be responsible not only for transferring the oil rights but which would also assist in the whole economic development of the area. What we have to work for is to give these people in the Middle East countries increasing control over their own natural resources, which in the first instance is oil.
If the western powers would take this type of imaginative approach we believe that many benefits could ensue. For one thing, it would wrest the initiative from the Soviet government and would reduce tension between east and west in so doing. It would help to offset the deep-rooted anti-western and anti-imperialist attitude which has made every past move on the part of western nations suspect among large sections of the Arab people. It would encourage Middle Eastern nations to develop along democratic lines and give them heart to throw out some of their despotic totalitarian rulers. We have countries in the Middle East where the great majority of the people live in poverty still, and a very small ruling class live in the lap of luxury, or I will say super luxury. Most important of all, it would raise the living standards of the Arab people and could lead to the transformation of Arab nationalism into a constructive world force for peace.

Supply-External Affairs
We are urging the government to give consideration to these proposals. As the last speaker on behalf of the opposition said, Canada can continue to play the role it is playing at the present time in the provision of UNEF, supplying the services of its countrymen to preserve peace in that area, and to act as an observer corps. It can also act in the assessment and the reporting of the situation in the Middle East, in counselling, advising and using its influence toward peace in the area.
Before concluding, I want to say a few words with respect to the use of nuclear weapons and nuclear warfare. The minister said in his speech this morning that the Canadian people are interested in foreign affairs, and I think that increased numbers of the people are very concerned about developing a policy which will work toward building world peace. As far as Canada is concerned, I think that most of the religious bodies have made strong representations in this respect. I know the Anglican church, of which I am a member, and the United church have passed resolutions, both at the national level and the diocesan or regional level. I have a cutting from the Ottawa Journal of Thursday, July 2 last where the pope warns "Peace or Destruction; first encyclical appeals to leaders 'Try every approach'". Then I have another clipping from the Globe and Mail of May 16 last where Rabbi Abraham Feinberg suggests that a congress of all faiths could help prevent the drift toward war. In the report of his speech, I read this statement by the Rabbi, Abraham Feinberg:
I believe that religion has a call to leadership, to make science the servant of man rather than of homicide-
I think they are very forceful and well expressed words. I mention these statements made on behalf of churches and religious leaders to show the tremendous support the government has for all it does in working toward the maintenance of world peace. It has support not only from our religious leaders but also from our scientists. I want to quote briefly from an article in the Gazette of Wednesday, June 3, 1959 reporting some remarks of Dr. O. M. Solandt, who I think at one time was chief of our defence research board. The article is headed, "Mankind Must Alter Behaviour", and it goes on:
Dr. O. M. Solandt, vice president in charge of research and development of the Canadian National Railways, said yesterday that a global nuclear war "would certainly be the end of our present civilization and could conceivably wipe out the human race as we know it."
Dr. Solandt, former head of Canada's defence research board, told a meeting of the Quebec Heart


Foundation at the Queen Elizabeth hotel that "both sides could deliver crippling blows in spite of the advantage of surprise that would go to the aggressor."
In a strong plea for more emphasis on changing mankind's behaviour than on improving his knowledge of the physical sciences, Dr. Solandt said: "This generation is faced with a problem unique in human history. If we are to ensure the survival of our civilization we must try to ensure that our children do not behave the way we behaved."
Then he goes on to stress the need for every effort to be made to develop world peace. I am certain that the government, in view of public opinion generally in the country, has the opportunity to provide leadership of the most fruitful kind, and to speak up for Canada in this respect. I refer particularly, of course, to the field of disarmament and nuclear weapons and weapon testing. It should not be necessary for me to tell the house more of the dreadful effects that a nuclear war would have on the whole of mankind; we are all well aware of the physical devastation which would result. We are slowly coming to realize more clearly the horrible dangers from radiation which would profoundly affect all life everywhere on this planet of ours, following upon such a holocaust. The very thought should be sufficient to cause all nations to cease this hideous arms race as regards nuclear weapons.
As we informed the house at this time last week, we shall do everything in our power to convince the government of the utter futility, the horrible folly, of allowing ourselves to contribute toward this mad race -I refer to the nuclear arms race-which, in the end can only culminate in suicidal destruction for all living creatures. I shall not pursue this particular point further. However, I should like to draw the attention of the minister and of the committee to an article entitled "A Primer on Fallout", which appears in the latest copy-July 9-of the Reporter magazine, and which I feel strongly all hon. members should read. It is written by people who know. It seems to be a most objective and factual account of nuclear fallout and of the dangers from nuclear radiation.
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to the minister's comments on the disarmament subcommittee. I hope that the committee will be reconvened and will continue to function. We wish him well in everything he does in his high office to prod that committee into meeting and to prod it into action. As long as the committees are meeting and people are talking and negotiating, I think this indicates that we are getting somewhere.
I understand the disarmament subcommittee of the United Nations, on which Canada is

one of five members, has not met since September, 1957. From the minister's comments of this morning with respect to this committee I know he will do all he can and will use his influence to get the committee meeting again and discussing this most important question in the hope of making some progress in the near future. It must be remembered that much has happened during the intervening period since the committee met. For one thing the meeting of experts held in Geneva last year issued a promising report on the technical aspects of nuclear detection and control. There has been some technical advance since the committee last met. Mr. Chairman, you must excuse me, but I lost my teeth owing to war disabilities and have false teeth which bobble around, and I am having a great deal of trouble this afternoon. I hope you will forgive me for that fact.
As I was saying, for one thing the meeting of experts held in Geneva last year issued a promising report on the technical aspects of nuclear detection and control which may be of some assistance to the subcommittee should they decide to meet. But they must meet and talk and discuss. This is what we feel the minister should initiate, promote and continue to work for, in view of the privileged position Canada still has as a member of that subcommittee. Fortunately we are a member of that subcommittee. Perhaps as the minister becomes better acquainted with the problems of disarmament -and there is no doubt that the minister will be learning from day to day-he will be in a stronger position to bring influence to bear on the cabinet in order that they review what must be, from our point of view, a panic decision to introduce nuclear weapons into Canada. He should do this from the conviction that it will have adverse affects on Canada's ability to assume a leading role which should be hers on the disarmament subcommittee in particular, generally in the United Nations and thus in the world at large. We urge the minister to use his good offices in that respect to the limit.
The government must act and be sustained on the basis of humanitarian principles, particularly in this most important and serious matter. Only then will the government be able to surmount the hurdles which these intricate and complex problems erect on the course toward action to peace.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Atlantic congress of the NATO parliamentary association was held in London, England from June 5 to 10 of this year. I had the privilege of acting as the honorary general secretary of the Canadian delegation, and I am very happy
Supply-External Affairs to report to the committee at this time on Canada's part at this important gathering.
As early as 1957 plans were proposed that in 1959, the tenth anniversary year of the treaty, there should be a general congress composed of parliamentarians and distinguished citizens from the nations of NATO. The whole purpose and theme of the congress was to bring together the most distinguished and able citizens representative of the principal aspects of the NATO countries-politics, industry, commerce, finance, labour, education, mass media et cetera-to consider ways and means of developing closer co-operation between North American and European members of NATO in the fields of political, economic and cultural as well as military affairs.
In brief, the congress was to provide an opportunity of examining, on the one hand, the record of the NATO countries as members of an alliance and the prospects of their development into partners in a community and, on the other hand, the problems of relations between the NATO countries and the free and uncommitted world, and relations between the NATO countries and the communist bloc. The congress brought together 650 delegates from 15 nations of the alliance, the delegations ranging in numbers from 130 from the United States to 10 from Luxembourg.
I should like to take a few moments of the time of the committee to discuss Canada's delegation. Headed by the hon. member for Saskatoon, Canada's delegation totalled 56 and included 18 members from the 3 parties in the House of Commons; 3 members from the other place, namely the hon. senator from Ottawa West and the hon. senator from Lumsden, plus the hon. senator from Lunenburg who was one of the co-founders of the NATO parliamentary association and is now the honorary life president of that body. Then we had 36 distinguished Canadian citizens from all walks of life:-from the church, industry, the universities, the professions, the arts and sciences, labour and so on.
It was unfortunate that the secretary-treasurer of the Canadian NATO parliamentary association, who is also the second clerk assistant of this House of Commons, was not able to accompany us. This gentleman had rendered yeoman service in the organization of the Canadian delegation and his knowledge and experience would have been of inestimable value to us. Naturally, he could not leave while the house was in session. For six months prior to our going to England, the head of the delegation and other officers of the Canadian association worked to complete the organization which was so necessary if we were to do the job as we should.

The writing of papers on the subjects to be discussed at the congress was one activity in which Canada also played its full part. No less than eight papers were written by Canadians. Especially fine ones were contributed by the head of our delegation, the hon. member for Saskatoon; by the senator from Ottawa West; by Mr. Edward Nelson, the president of the united farmers of Alberta and others.
The work of the congress was divided into five major committees. These committees were as follows. The spiritual and cultural committee which was divided into 3 subcommittees; 1. moral and spiritual values of the Atlantic community; 2. information and education program; and 3. Atlantic institute. The political committee chaired, as I said earlier, by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris having as its subcommittees: 1. co-ordination of policies and settlement of disputes; 2. Atlantic institutions; and 3. military questions. The economic committee with its sub-committees: 1. resources and underdeveloped areas in the Atlantic countries; 2. scientific and technical co-operation; 3. implications of western European economic integration; 4. freedom of trade and problems of exchange and stability. The free world committee with its sub-committees: 1. conflict and community of interests; 2. common political policies of the west; 3. common economic policies of the west. The communist bloc committee with its sub-committees; 1. political policies; 2. economic policies; 3. soviet and western propaganda techniques. There was also, of course, the declarations committee whose report I plan later to read into the minutes of this session.
The congress was officially opened by Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II in the Great Westminster Hall beside the abbey. Plenary sessions were held, as I have mentioned, in Church House. Mr. Chairman, recently I too had the privilege of attending the NATO congress in London, on June 3 last, and I would like to take a few minutes to tell the house the few personal impressions that I have kept from that meeting.
That congress of the nations which are grouped in the Atlantic community was held for the purpose, in my opinion, of reviewing the whole concept of NATO since its creation in 1949.
To achieve that purpose, the congress acted on six basic principles which, while summing up the action of NATO since its foundation, could also provide the organization with the necessary leadership to fulfil the objectives arising out of present requirements and in this way, adequately meet the views of member nations in the military, economic, political, social and scientific fields.

Supply-External Affairs
It is impossible for me, in the short time I have at my disposal, to comment on all the resolutions adopted by the congress, following the discussion of the principles I have mentioned. However, I would like to indicate the work and the important findings of the committee whose duty it was to make recommendations to the general assembly on matters of spiritual and cultural concern.
Following the committee's suggestions, the congress adopted the four following points:
1.	That the member states of NATO take efficient counter measures in order to fight against the Soviet ideological war, and that a formal international organization of free nations be established for the distribution of information towards that end.
2.	That it would be advisable to create a study centre of the Atlantic community to serve as information bureau and intellectual centre.
3.	That there should be greater integration of scientific research and particularly, of pure research.
4.	That it is advisable to strengthen and to expand the forms of action in the field of information and education, in order to impress more deeply in the minds and the hearts of the nations the meaning of the Atlantic community and its spiritual and moral principles.
Those resolutions clearly show that NATO must not limit itself to military considerations, but that the Atlantic community must also create organizations that would be able to think and to spread among free nations the ideas and the moral and intellectual concepts of member nations that want to work within the spirit and the framework of NATO.
What the Atlantic community wants to defend- said Mr. Jean Danielou, the French delegate,
-is not a particular civilization against another particular civilization; it is civilization period, of which the Atlantic community is the expression.
The Atlantic community, Mr. Chairman, should therefore be organized so as to be able to stand up to communist propaganda whose purpose is to attack and destroy the principle of liberty of nations that still believe in the peaceful co-existence of the peoples of mankind.
The great danger which the free nations of the world have to face today is communist propaganda in all its forms. At present the Soviets have 500,000 individuals at their service to make this propaganda system work, and they are spending 2 billion dollars a year to try and subvert a billion free men. Moscow is therefore spending $2 a year for each free human being it wants to subjugate. A U.S. ' senate commission recently informed us, as a matter of fact,

that the United States allow 1J cent a year per capita for their world propaganda.
Those figures clearly indicate that it is high time for the free nations to get together to meet the Soviet menace and fight the ideological warfare of the U.S.S.R.
During the congress, we heard pressing appeals made by several delegates, on the urgency of the situation. I remember, among others, the appeal of Mrs. Suzanne Lahin, who said:
I urge the delegates to open their eyes. The danger is a pressing and acute one, and it is dramatically urgent that the West should wake up, pull itself together, put all its intellectual and material resources to work and, rousing itself on the very fringe of the abyss it should not only avoid losing the cold war, but try to win it as well. It is just as fatal to die of cold as it is to die of burns. Our defeat would be particularly tragic in that the democratic West would die from a paralysis of the very things that once made its greatness.
In view of those facts so frequently expressed at the meeting, NATO decided to proceed with the creation of the Atlantic institute, or more accurately of an Atlantic community study centre which would serve as an information service and intellectual centre.
The Atlantic institute would exercise a certain number of duties, it would undertake certain projects on its own and co-operate with existing organizations in respect of certain others.
It would favour and support human exchange between the western nations, in order to contribute to greater mutual understanding. It would supply the machinery for the meeting not only of academic and intellectual people, but of leaders in every walk of life in order to stimulate a new knowledge with regard to problems of common concern.
The institute would serve as a clearing house and, on request, as co-ordinating centre for operations and projects connected with its basic interests. It would also initiate and support educational activities designed to promote understanding and to apply the concept of the Atlantic community.
It is in that spirit that the parties to the North Atlantic Treaty, in 1949, indicated the wider concept they had in mind when they referred, in article 2 of the charter, to the need for a better understanding of the underlying principles of the free institutions of the community.
Canada has played an important part in that congress and, in that connection, I

should like to quote from a report published in La Presse of July 4, 1959, and written by Mr. Roger Champoux, a newspaperman and Canadian delegate to the Congress:
People will ask what part Canada has played in this meeting of the free world, this soul-searching by 14 countries integrated into the most powerful alliance in the present world.
It was an outstanding part, because Canada is no longer a dependent country. Thanks to its highly informed and active delegates, Canada ranked high, and contributions by Canadian delegates drew attention; the same applies to the suggestions made by a number of delegates.
Speeches were made by several delegates, and the tasks assigned to a number of us were done quickly, efficiently and with a degree of integrity that was commended in the highest terms.
Mr. Chairman, Canada is no longer and will never be a silent partner in world meetings. It is realized in Europe that our country, whose stature always causes amazement, has become the pivot of a disturbed world, anxiously in search of a firm basis, a solid support and a reliable ally.
I can therefore fairly say, in closing, that this congress has deepened my understanding of international problems and has provided me with an opportunity of acquiring experience that will long stand me in good stead. (Text):

Mr. Chairman, before I venture upon the few observations I wish to make at this time I should like to express the gratification I felt when the announcement was made of the appointment of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to his present position. Hon. members will realize that the minister is held in respect and affection in his native province, and those feelings were mingled with pride at the knowledge that he would be guiding the foreign policy of the people of this country in the councils of the world.
When the announcement was made two and a half weeks ago that Canada was undertaking a special program with respect to the clearance of the refugee camps in Europe during this world refugee year, was considering new lines of approach to some of the problems that have been outstanding throughout the 14 years since the war, there was unanimous approval of the announcement in this house and I believe a general acceptance and approval across the country.
Hon. members will recognize, and I trust the people of Canada are persuaded, that the circumstances that have brought about the existence in Europe, in the Middle East and in the Far East of large numbers of homeless people, refugees, are a condemnation of the nations from which they have fled; but as long as they continue to exist in camps, or in other accommodations, unsettled, unaccepted, and, indeed, in many cases, unacceptable, then their existence under those
Supply-External Affairs circumstances is a reproach to the western nations to whom they have turned for haven. Therefore, I feel certain that there cannot be other than reason for congratulations to the government that it has decided to take certain steps to try to meet the problems of at least some of these people.
We know that among the hundreds of thousands of refugees there are those who at least still have their health; that given time, given favourable opportunities, they may find countries in the world that will accept them, where they can be assimilated, where they can once more stand on their own feet and find their own places in the world; but there are also many, far too many, unfortunately, who suffer from disability, or from illness, that makes it impossible for them to escape the conditions under which they now live because the illness or the disability makes them unacceptable in so many countries.
We in Canada have one of the best records in the world in so far as assistance in providing new homes for refugees is concerned, but we have not perhaps done as much as we might have done for those who are classified in United Nations parlance as difficult cases. In the minister's announcement there was reference specifically to tubercular cases. Those people face the most difficult situation of all; for there are relatively few places in the world where they are provided for, or where they are now accepted. Here in Canada there is, as all hon, members realize, a special difficulty in that the government of Canada itself has no hospital in which it can take care of such people, even if they came here; that any such hospitals as exist in the country come under provincial jurisdiction, and we can only introduce tubercular refugees into these hospitals if the provinces will agree to accept them. Therefore, I hope that in this year, when so much attention has been focused on the problems of refugees, the provincial authorities can be persuaded and will be willing to consider the possibility of accepting in each province where available space can be provided at least a number of the tubercular cases among the refugees in Europe today.
In solving the problems of any one tubercular refugee it often happens that the problem of a whole family is solved; for if any single member of a family unit is suffering from the disease they are not now acceptable to us. But if we accept the one, then it may be automatically supposed we will accept the rest of the family; the united family group can come into the country and that problem is solved for a deserving group of people who at the present time have very little hope. However, there have been indications during this year that this problem

Supply-External Affairs is receiving wider recognition than it has received in the past. In February the government of New Zealand accepted 20 handicapped refugees with their families, and in May the government of Sweden, which has done so much to pioneer the acceptance of tubercular refugees, accepted a further group of 54.
It may be pointed out that over the years that Sweden has been providing a haven for tubercular refugees, 649 cases altogether have been provided for in that country, and, with their dependants, a solution has been found for the problems of 1,500 people. Of that number only 649 were actually tubercular. It was reported at the 13th session of the United Nations last fall that in one particular group of 200 which was taken from the camps by Sweden and Denmark in conjunction, a group that included as well as tubercular cases some mental cases, there had been complete recovery and assimilation of that total number of 200.
It is not as though in undertaking such a program Canada would be embarking upon unknown ground. There is the example of Sweden, Denmark, New Zealand and the other countries which are dealing in difficult cases which we may follow, and from which we can gain experience and perhaps learn to avoid any pitfalls that may be inherent in such a plan. Therefore, the principle of the thing has been accepted by the government. I only hope now that every effort will be made to give it practical realization. I hope that the people of Canada will support this program; that the provincial governments will provide the necessary facilities, the facilities that only they can provide, and that perhaps in this way, at a time when considerations of compassion and humanity are so important in an unsettled world, this program will prove successful and provide the solution of the problems of people who now live with very little hope.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take a few minutes to mention certain matters. Along with other members who have preceded me I also want to wish the minister well in his new responsibility. His new department possibly involves more responsibility than any other department. Canadians will long remember his remarks of this morning when he said, if I have his words right, that in this nuclear age war is unthinkable and there simply is no alternative to continued negotiation. I hope I have his words right. I believe they will obtain for the minister the best wishes of 17J million Canadians. We have every confidence that the minister is going to continue to pursue that philosophy as long as he holds his present high office.
I wish to refer to a couple of matters which the minister may consider as relatively minor but which to me are of rather important significance. I should like to compliment the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke on the great interest he has exhibited over the past year or more in the question of the refugees of the world. Most Canadians recognize that we are either refugees or the sons, grandsons or greatgrandsons of refugees. Most of our forefathers left European shores because they found life and conditions unbearable there and they were political, religious or some other type of refugees.
I believe that we may have been following a wrong policy with respect to refugees in that in our openheartedness we have only been willing to supply money for the maintenance of refugees in other parts of the world. I know that money can salve our

consciences at times but in my opinion the move that was made a number of weeks ago when the government announced its willingness to accept a certain number of these refugees into Canada was a welcome one. However, I believe it was a very limited move indeed and I hope that in the months ahead the government will give serious consideration to ending once and for all the refugee camp problem existing in Europe and that we will not only be willing to accept into Canada cases involving tuberculosis merely because we happen to have empty sanitaria space but will also be willing to accept our fair share of the refugees still in camps in Europe 14 years after the end of the second world war. I hope that we will take our share and have an end to this continuing problem in Europe.
I also fail to appreciate Canada's continued willingness to pay money toward the maintenance of the refugee camp in the Middle East because the problem there is not being resolved by our continuing to feed, clothe and supply education, housing and medical care to these people. Even today there are several hundred thousand more refugees in the Middle East than there were after the formation of Israel. I believe that Canada should follow an aggressive policy in the United Nations toward the re-establishment of these refugees. I regret to have to inform the minister that I have spoken to a number of Canadians who have actually visited the refugee camps and who say that the state of demoralization that has now come about is simply deplorable. These people have been nursed, fed and supplied with all their basic needs, even though at a very minimum level, but some of them have now become so lazy that they are even unwilling to lift their hands to swipe away the flies that are feeding on their eyes.
I believe that if Canadians continue to endorse this refugee camp and the existing arrangements we will not be making our maximum contribution. In my opinion Canada should not only be willing to accept a number of these people into our country but Canada should follow a policy at the United Nations that will lead to the re-establishment of these refugees possibly in some of the arid regions of the Middle East which can be made into useful areas.
Another refugee problem exists, as the minister well knows, on the island of Hong Kong. I feel that the minister might use his good offices with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration so that Canadians of Chinese origin with near relatives in Hong Kong would have a little less tortuous path to pursue in obtaining the right to bring these people, who are refugees from the mainland
Supply-External Affairs of China, into Canada. The Canadian people, as the minister knows, are an open and kindhearted people and with respect to the whole question of refugees the minister will always find that the people of Canada will support him in any progressive move he can make.
Another policy about which I feel I have to complain a little is that involving the urging of Canadians to adopt an orphan overseas and to send $15, $20 or $30 a month to maintain an orphan in some other area of the world. I feel that orphans are the best possible kind of immigrant we can have in Canada, and once again I would like to appeal to the minister to use his influence with his colleague, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, to pursue a policy whereby all these orphans might benefit by encouraging the foster father, the foster mother or foster parents not to supply money to maintain the orphan overseas but rather to bring the orphan into Canada and to look after the orphan in their own home.
I would also like to appeal to the minister to do a little bit of investigating as to what happened to what the newspapers reported about a year ago was the Prime Minister's plan for a possible agreement between Canada and the U.S.S.R. whereby Canada and the Soviet union might agree upon an Arctic inspection plan and thereby eliminate the need for the vast armament expenditures within the Arctic areas. We have never had a report in the House of Commons as to why that plan suddenly disappeared. We have never had a report on the plan at all. I believed at the time I first read of it that the plan was an excellent idea, enough to be explored to the full, and I hope that the minister at some time will pay some attention to that and see whether or not it was the United States government that completely vetoed the plan and caused the Canadian government immediately to forget it, and also investigate whether or not it should be revived.
I would also like to appeal to the minister to pay some little attention to the quality of Canadians parliamentary representation abroad. I have been at a number of international gatherings, and I have always been very impressed with the quality of representatives at these international gatherings who came from either Washington or Westminster. I have always had the feeling that when Canada is asked to send 15 members of parliament here, five members of parliament there, and eight members of parliament somewhere else to international meetings, far too often what happens in effect is that the least able members of the House of Commons, the ones who are not needed at home, are

I should like to express my appreciation to the minister at this time for going to considerable trouble in arranging for a representative of Canadian teachers to attend the meeting now taking place in London in connection with the establishment of a commonwealth scholarship program. I noted the minister said this morning that the Canadian government expected that it would have to spend about $1 million a year on this type of proposal, and that out of a thousand scholarships we would be expected to look after roughly 250 of them. I do not want to be too inquisitive, but it looks like a rather openhearted amount, $4,000 per year for each of them. Unless the overhead is unduly large, I feel that this is an amount which can hardly be compared with even a Rhodes scholarship or an I.O.D.E. scholarship. They certainly do not amount to $4,000 a year, yet the minister indicated there would be 250 scholarships at a cost of roughly $1 million.
I was a little disappointed at the amount which was announced. I had hoped that Canada would be prepared to spend at least $10 million or $20 million on this type of enterprise, and that Canadian universities and other institutions of learning might expect to receive not 250 but more in the neighbourhood of 2,500 commonwealth students who would be obtaining their education here. However, I heartily endorse the program. Our whole group heartily endorse this program. We only regret that it is not more extensive. However, we realize it is only the beginning and that it may be expanded in the years ahead. We feel that it is very important that the commonwealth nations help each other in this manner and thereby help to spread some of the traditions


that we hope will become firmly rooted in all areas of the British commonwealth of nations.
I have never expressed this sentiment in the house before. However, I would like to inform the minister that my great grandfather and my grandfather, upon the ascension of Mr. Bismarck in Europe, left European shores and chose liberty under the traditions which were established and recognized as the basic liberties of the individual in areas where the Union Jack was known. I personally would like to see a spread of this liberty, but not by imposition. We must realize that we have to live in a world with many others who have different attitudes and approaches to many of our main problems in life. However, we should by example help in every way we can to spread the basic traditions that have made the commonwealth, and especially the heart of the commonwealth, the United Kingdom, even though it may not be militarily powerful any more, into the most respected nation today in the world. I believe that the establishment of a commonwealth scholarship program will help very much toward the accomplishment of this aim that I am sure all members of this house endorse.
