Mr. Chairman, if I venture to take part in this debate, it is not so much that I am aware of the scope and difficulty of the subject-matter, but I consider it important for us members to discuss external affairs, certainly not as experts, but as representatives of the people. Indeed, it is our responsibility to inform those we represent of what is happening in diplomatic circles and on the international scene. Moreover, it is our duty to keep the government aware of the popular reaction to the international situation and to its own policy.
Hon. members must recall what is ultimately at stake in the secret struggle taking place at the diplomatic level. What is at stake is indeed the very survival of civilization and freedom for the preservation of peace. It is also our responsibility as members to remind the public that every single individual will ultimately reap the sweet or bitter fruit of official high level policy.
My intentions are of modest scope. I simply want to reaffirm what seems to me fundamental in the matter. But before dealing with the subject, I would like, if I may, Mr. Chairman, to tender my warmest congratulations to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). The way in which the announcement of his appointment to his present post was received told him, better than I can, the very great esteem in

which he is regarded by his colleagues. I want to tell him, perhaps on behalf of the younger members in this house, that we admire him very sincerely and that since our arrival in this House of Commons, he has been to us a model and an example. Because of his great kindness, his simplicity and sincerity, we would be inclined to consider him as a father if, on the other hand, his very great cordiality, did not make us consider him, instead, as an older brother. At all events, Mr. Chairman, together with all my fellow members, I welcome this appointment which, I am sure, will have happiest results for Canada. Mr. Chairman, last autumn, I had the honour to be invited to attend the 13th general assembly of the United Nations as Canadian delegate. I must say that my stay in New York has taught me a very great lesson. I was able to realize, on the spot, the importance of diplomatic debate and the efficient part played there by Canada. I listened, day by day to debates on the most vital principles. And, when I was a member of the fifth commission -the administrative and budgetary commission-I could see all the underlying factors of international policy coming up in the discussions, in the form of estimates introduced for approval. I was thus able to familiarize myself with external affairs and to understand the extreme difficulty of some situations and the importance of those discussions.
Today-and even more so today than before -the international situation cannot but cause the gravest misgivings, Mr. Chairman. If we remember the Middle East crisis in the summer of 1958, as well as the Quemoy and Matsu islands issue we realize that the events which troubled the world at that time made us fear the worse conflicts. Since then, there has been a settlement. It nevertheless remains that this settlement has a precarious character because of the very strategic withdrawals which made it possible, but which leave the positions with regard to principle absolutely unchanged in the two camps.
The recent Berlin crisis proved that the international situation is not yet settled and that security and world peace are still threatened at this time. As a matter of fact, the Berlin crisis is a menace which, according to experts, might very well be the final test of strength. Its character is tragic mainly because of the fact that it again brings a major issue to the fore. It throws new light on events that seemed already old, but which are again emerging as a stark reality. These events were those that marked the end of
Supply-External Affairs the 1939-45 war, and they are the consequences of the negotiations held at the time.
Mr. Chairman, what impresses me and what I want to stress when I consider those international events, is the meaning and the interpretation we are forced to give them.
Indeed, we are actually in a position of perpetual conflict opposing-one might as well admit it-communists and non-communists. That masked, underhand conflict has degenerated into what is now called the cold war. It is none the less extremely important and dangerous; as witness the various international developments to which I referred a moment ago. All those developments are increasing international tension and threatening the world with a menace of which our young men will perhaps suffer the dire consequences one of these days.
Those facts, which in reality constitute the international crisis, are an indication of Russia's and her satellites' intentions, and they reveal the character of the philosophy behind their diplomatic approach.
The heart of the problem lies in that opposition commonly called: East-West opposition. It lies in this fact that a fight, a fight to the finish, so it seems, is being waged between communist and non-communist countries. That opposition is one of principles, because it involves two opposite philosophies, two opposite civilizations, and because it is based on contradictory principles. It opposes an atheistic civilization to a civilization of faith, a deistic civilization; it sets a materialistic civilization against one based on the principle of priority of spiritual matters; a form of communism against a normal form of individualism; social planning against private enterprise, arbitrary state control against divine right, natural right. Also, if we care to take a closer and more realistic look at the matter, we realize that we are faced with opposition between tyranny and freedom.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the major objective that we must pursue, is the defence of our civilization, western and Christian civilization. The result will be a struggle not for geographical possessions, not for military supremacy, not for economic domination, nor for political hegemony, but a struggle for the survival of a civilization, its development and perfection. That struggle must be considered by us as of capital importance, since our civilization, which we seek to defend, must be rooted in fundamental principles which are like the mainstays of our lives; those principles are based on divine right, natural right, on freedom of the individual, and on individual and social ethics. It is a

Supply-External Affairs civilization which has historic achievements to its credit: its philosophy, its culture, its letters and its arts, its technology and science in all its forms. Consequently, it is that objective we must defend. We are defending acknowledged values, values which have been historically established and, in my opinion, that is an approach we should never lose sight of in any consideration of external affairs.
The defence of western civilization is not therefore based on sentimental reasons but on historic realities. I was saying a moment ago that this civilization we are defending is opposed by a materialistic civilization that can certainly produce astonishing technological achievements, and may even bring about a certain amount of well-being, but at an extremely heavy cost, the loss of individual freedom in exchange for purely material progress.
Under the circumstances, Mr. Chairman, our attitude must be a practical and realistic one, in view of the threat of war and particularly of a nuclear war that would dwarf any catastrophe ever recorded. Our attitude must be one of strength, and must prompt us to look for the facts behind the threats from Russia and the satellite countries, but it must above all be one of caution so that we may exhaust every diplomatic means at our disposal. In that regard, our membership in the United Nations and in NATO should always be viewed as a way of cooperating in the maintenance of world peace and security.
There are people today who favour cooperation in every field with those whom we must rightfully consider as enemies of our civilization. Such a policy might be largely a matter of political and diplomatic strategy; it might in some ways, yield excellent results, but it should not cause us to lose sight of the major principles involved. Fear of war must not make us lose sight of our goal, which is the defence of the values underlying our way of life and our community.
The Canadian government, through its membership in the UN and in NATO, must maintain a defence system and must, in cooperation with its neighbours and with the major countries of NATO, keep up a highly efficient protection system. That, of course, involves considerable expense, and it is our duty, as representatives of the people, to


explain to the people that Canada's defence system involves a measure of sacrifice on the part of the nation and its citizens.
Quite often, we hear complaints, we hear all kinds of criticism on the efforts Canada has to make to expand its defence system. It is our job to explain the meaning of that protection, which inevitably costs money.
However, it seems to me that there is one area where Canada's effort should be greater, and I refer to the help Canada must or has agreed to provide to underdeveloped countries. In countries of Africa and Asia, and in some countries nearer to us, there are people today who are yearning for social improvement and for greater personal and political freedom. To reach those goals, however, they need technical, financial and cultural help. Such is the context for our contribution to the various schemes aimed at helping underdeveloped countries.
I, for my part, know that this undertaking of the Canadian government has often been harshly criticized; but this criticism, which might in some cases be justified, is easily refuted-and this again is a responsibility of those who represent the people-provided we take the trouble of making the public understand that they are part of the family of man, of pointing out the interdependence of Canadian citizens and of all the citizens of the world who sincerely want to promote the cause of peace.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I want to point out that just about everywhere in Canada there may be agents of disorder, agents who may be propagandists of subversive ideas. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) stressed today, some of these agents try to undermine our social and political institutions in Canada and are therefore, in fact, distributors of subversive political propaganda.
Those agents are preventing the creation and the implementation of defence and diplomatic policy which would be really efficient and produce all the results we expect of it.
We, in Canada, have a particular role to play; we must show the way we must set for other nations-more so perhaps because we are a young nation-the example of a true to life civilization which, to all practical intents, proves the historical and intrinsic value of the principles that we consider as the basis of Christian and western civilization. The hon. member for Essex East mentioned the importance of the forthcoming session of the United Nations which will be opening in September. I can assure him that I intend to lead the Canadian delegation at this session and will stay in New York as long as possible. However, there are various duties which come up from time to time in Canada or perhaps in some other part of the world and as the hon. member knows it is impossible for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to be there for the whole of the duration of the session.
The hon. member mentioned the need for increased representation for Canada in the Middle East, referring particularly to Iraq. This is under consideration by the department. As the hon. gentleman said, there has been a mission set up in Iran. I believe the intention had been to have a charge d'affaires in Iraq. Then there was trouble in that country about a year ago. I am not yet in a position to announce just what steps the government can take. Our ambassador to the United Arab Republic will be going to Baghdad in a few days to attend the anniversary of the revolution of last year which was on July 14 and while there no doubt he will be able to look into the whole situation. I should like the hon. member for Essex East to realize that we are interested in the possibilities of establishing a further mission in this area which has been and is of such great importance in world affairs.
I shall not comment on the hon. member's quotations from the London Times. That, of course, is a great newspaper. I remember reading it with great confidence 45 years ago. But like all other newspapers it is not always right and perhaps the article from which he quoted was not as praiseworthy as he seemed to suggest.
He also mentioned the possibility of arrangements being made for what he called the United Nations presence in Berlin. There have been suggestions made that if the four negotiating powers could reach agreement then there might be a role for the

It may be that the solution of the Berlin problem will be along that line. At the moment, however, I am not in a position to take any stand one way or the other.
The hon. member for Kootenay West advanced many suggestions and outlined the policy of his party on various questions having to do with foreign policy. I know he will not expect me to comment on these policies. He said he felt that Canada had lost her contacts in world affairs and hoped that we would now resume these lost contacts. I can assure the hon. member that the losses have not been as great as he thinks. I should be very much surprised if any contacts whatever had been lost. Perhaps he was reading speculative articles in some of the newspapers as well when he formed that opinion.
The foreign service of Canada has an excellent standing all over the world. He would be surprised at the number and the quality of the dispatches which come in to the minister of the department every day from all over the world although I do not think that perhaps more than 10 per cent of the total volume would be passed on to me. I can assure the hon. gentleman that Canada is very well represented in all parts of the world and I believe her standing in world affairs is as high as that of any other nation.
There are reasons for that, of course, beyond our own good qualities as Canadians. We are not in the position of having any past to explain nor do we have a record of wanting anybody's territory or of having designs on anybody. Our main ambition is to be friendly with all other nations and I believe that is characteristic of the Canadian outlook. This has been one reason why we have enjoyed such a high standing, as well, of course, as the fact that Canada has been very well served abroad not only on an official level but also in the public men who have represented this nation.
The hon. member need not be afraid that Canadian foreign policy will be merely a reflection of United States policy. We have great friendship and vast admiration for our cousins but we intend to stand on our own feet in foreign policy and try to take the approach which the average Canadian would take on these questions.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury and the hon. member for Charlevoix made very interesting reports on the Atlantic congress

In this connection I find it exceedingly difficult to believe that the remarks made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam about the rather inferior calibre of the Canadian representatives at conferences were made seriously. It may be that the Canadian representatives are not expert on protocol. I find it quite a problem myself and I think any Canadian would until he had been in the diplomatic service for a lifetime. The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke made a very thoughtful and appealing speech on the refugee problem. This was also dealt with by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. We are very interested to see just what the reaction of the Canadian people will be to the suggestion that a real attempt be made to get at the hard core of this refugee problem. If this is to be done it will mean bringing people to Canada who are not in good physical condition; it will cost money and it will require understanding on the part of our own Canadian people.
When I suggested a week or two ago that we were prepared to embark on a program that would help to meet this refugee problem I was not just sure what the reaction would be. So far it has been excellent, very gratifying, and the remarks made by these two gentlemen today will help a great deal to make it possible for Canada to adopt a worthwhile policy to deal with this situation.
The hon. member for Lapointe made a suggestion that Canada should have diplomatic representation in Ethiopia and others have come forward with the same proposal. We have always enjoyed the friendliest of relations with Ethiopia. Hon. members will recall, for instance, the welcome visit to Canada of His Majesty, the Emperor of Ethiopia, in 1954. The question of establishing diplomatic relations with this country is, of course, kept under review in the light of the requirements of Canadian citizens in Ethiopia and of the various demands on our financial and personnel resources.
As hon. members know, this department operates on cold, hard cash, and we always have to consider whether we can get the money to establish those missions. It is not simply a case of deciding that we would like a mission here and a mission there, and establishing them. We have to do business with the treasury board, just as do the other departments, and in my experience treasury board is sometimes quite a high hurdle to get over.


To get back to Ethiopia, I might say that the registration of such Canadians with the United Kingdom embassy in Addis Ababa is a normal practice in countries where Canada has no diplomatic mission, and this practice has proved to be generally satisfactory.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam referred to the plan proposed by our own Prime Minister for inspection of Arctic regions, both of Canada and of the Soviet union, and he seemed to think that that plan had been put away in a filing cabinet and forgotten; but such is not the case. Canada was associated with the original proposal of a regional disarmament inspection zone in Arctic areas. No agreement has been reached with the Soviet union on such an area, but the Canadian government remains today ready to co-operate fully in any such plan that may be worked out between the nations.
That hon. member also mentioned the cost per student under the commonwealth education plan. The meetings to discuss the details of such a plan will not be held until next week. The figure of $1 million is an estimate. However, I point out that these students will be graduates taking post-graduate courses, and that the cost will include travel, maintenance and contributions to the universities. Also, of course, Canada will have to pay her share of the administrative expenses in connection with the plan. But the hon. member can be quite sure that there will be no money thrown away. In my experience this seldom happens under any scholarship plan.
Finally, the hon. member for Roberval made a very thought-provoking speech, as he always does, and his comments, too, will be given very careful consideration by myself and by the officials of the department.
I think that covers many of the points which were raised by the different members, and I shall be very glad to try to answer any other questions as we go through the estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I thought perhaps I might have made my remarks with regard to this item on item 1, but I find that perhaps they will be more appropriate under this heading. I think that our country should be a little more concerned than is manifest about the Suez canal difficulty which is interfering with world shipping. Canada is gradually becoming more of a chartering country than ever before. Our merchant marine is not as effective or as new as it was. We have pretty nearly disposed of our entire merchant marine and shipping companies I imagine are resorting more and more to the use of chartered bottoms for the shipping of Canadian goods throughout the world. I think it is an undue interference by any one country to dictate to other countries in the world who they can and cannot deal with, and I think the government should perhaps express itself on this question.
I think there is no necessity for anyone to discuss the importance of freedom of the seas, which is an important part of shipping rights. If this is interfered with, certainly our shipping capacity or our trade is interfered with; and because our trade is interfered with I think Canada should take some stand, either through the United Nations or otherwise. It is true that the secretary general is over there now attempting to iron out these things but I think the hand of the secretary general would be much strengthened if countries requiring the freedom of the seas and the use of the seas for their trade would express themselves. Perhaps some form of protest is being transmitted to which publicity is not given. But I feel that a country like Canada which has always championed the rights of free trade and the right of using the high seas should most certainly now take some stand. We depend upon the right to use the sea. We depend not only on Canadian vessels but upon foreign vessels and chartered vessels. I think we shall be seriously prejudiced if we do not speak up for them.
I have the feeling that our representative at the United Nations should be especially briefed on this subject. When there was difficulty in the Middle East it will be recalled that troops were withdrawn, peace was adjusted, and armistice was created, one condition which was that the Suez Canal and the gulf of Tiran would be kept free for shipping. There has been an invasion of that condition. I think that Egypt has not lived

Supply-External Affairs up to her obligation as to which she gave a pledge to the United Nations. I am drawing this matter to the attention of the minister who, I realize, will be facing this problem now himself and urging him to take the stand, on the lofty level that our country has always taken, to see that right should prevail; that the freedom of the seas, above all, should be maintained; and that Canada's foreign trade should not be interrupted by the intransigence of any one country.

No. When I was speaking earlier, Mr. Chairman, I had casually mentioned the international court of justice and I had indicated that the president of the United States and the vice president, Mr. Nixon, had in the past few months made rather important statements with regard to the compulsory jurisdiction of the court and the position of the government of the United States in connection with this particular matter.
Since the end of the second world war, as compared with the situation that attended the court under the covenant, I think there has been a tendency-in which our country has participated-for countries to avoid opportunities of recourse to the international court of justice for the settlement of their disputes. I think that Canada ought to join with the United States in seeking to give this matter of compulsory jurisdiction at least further consideration, notwithstanding the attending difficulties.
Part of this problem, of course, is expressed in the reservations to the optional clause of the statute of the court as stated in article 36 of the statute, where states are permitted to submit to the jurisdiction of the court subject to certain reservations. In the case of Canada, in 1929 we made a declaration containing a number of reservations that perhaps have less relevance today than they had at that time. The situation under which we are prepared to accept the jurisdiction of the court is attended by certain reservations and certain conditions. We will accept the jurisdiction of the court where there is reciprocity, where there is ratification and where there is reservation as to a time limit. Then we also have made reservations as to other possible methods of settlement to which the parties have agreed to have recourse. Of course there is the reservation as to domestic jurisdiction and the reservation excluding disputes arising before the making of a declaration.
I suggest to the minister that I think the time has come to look at our position with regard to this situation, and to try and give the court increased status by giving it more to do. I think we might perhaps meet the problem involved in the domestic jurisdiction

clause by realizing that many matters of domestic jurisdiction now have become of serious international concern. In any event, I think that Canada ought not to be behind the United States in a matter of this sort. It does not mean that we have to make a final decision but we ought to make at least a pronouncement as strong as that made by the vice president of the United States, one which I think would give much encouragement to those who believe in the gradual building up of the processes of law and adjudication in international affairs.

At six o'clock my colleague from Essex East brought up what I consider to be an important question in connection with the use of the world court. I should like to support what he said and express the hope in doing so that this would perhaps be a suitable initiative for the Canadian government or a delegation of the Canadian government to pursue at an appropriate place, and I think the appropriate place might well be the forthcoming assembly of the United Nations.
Last April the vice president of the United States, I think at the Academy of Sciences at Princeton university made a speech which in my opinion was of considerable significance and in which he put forward this idea. It was a speech which obviously had the support of the United States administration because it had been referred to in approving terms by the attorney general and, indeed, the president himself has mentioned it. I should like to quote one paragraph from this speech:
We-
Meaning the United States.
-should take the Initiative in urging that in any future agreements provision be included to effect, one, that disputes which may arise as to the interpretation of the agreement should be submitted to the international court of justice at The Hague and, two, that the nations signing the agreement should be bound by the decision of the court in such cases.
Supply-External Affairs
This means that in any international agreements which may be made in the future there should be a clause to the effect that the signatories of the agreement would be bound by the decision of the international court of justice with respect to any dispute which might arise with regard to its interpretation. That would be one step in putting international law behind international policy.
I know that if the United States puts forward a proposal of this kind at the United Nations it would be suspect in the sense that it might become mixed up in the cold war and power politics and all sorts of things like that. But if a middle power, a power with a reputation such as Canada has, felt that this was a good proposal and felt that it should be followed up and put forward formally at a United Nations Assembly, that might be a very useful thing to do.
Possibly there are arguments against this proposal of which I am not aware, and the minister may wish to say a word about that. I am not asking him, naturally, to make any statement of government policy at this time, but I am asking him to give consideration to this question.

speechtext:
The points raised by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Essex East, while they both deal with the international court of Justice, are quite different in context. I have the answer now to the questions asked this afternoon by the hon. member for Essex East.
There appears to be a rather widespread feeling that the international court has fallen somewhat short of expectations. This is not due to any lack of high qualifications among the 15 judges of the court, who represent the main forms of civilization and the principal legal systems of the world. Rather, this feeling seems to stem from the fact that in the past 13 years there have been only 30 contentious cases submitted to the court and many of these have been stricken from the list due to objections made to the court's jurisdiction. We should, of course, remember that during this same period the international court delivered 10 advisory opinions. It is none the less difficult to dispute the fact that the machinery of the court has not been sufficiently employed either by the United Nations or by the member states themselves.
Recently, there have been signs of a resurgence of interest in the court's work. In the United States there have been suggestions by the United States attorney general, the vice president and by President Eisenhower himself that the United States should reexamine its relationship to the international court, particularly as regards the domestic jurisdiction reservation attached to its declaration accepting the compulsory jurisdiction of

Supply-External Affairs the international court. This reservation excludes disputes with regard to matters which are essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of the United States as determined by the United States. Now, that is a very big reservation which was made by the United States.
Canada does not have a reservation of this kind. The Canadian declaration accepting the compulsory jurisdiction of the international court excludes disputes with regard to questions which by international law fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of the dominion of Canada. In other words, we leave it to the international court to decide whether it has jurisdiction in any particular case and we do not reserve to ourselves the determination of whether the matter falls within domestic jurisdiction. It is to be hoped that in the future more and more states will come to accept the compulsory jurisdiction of the court with a minimum of reservation.
With regard to the aspect raised by the Leader of the Opposition, this proposal is being studied in the department at the present time. It brings up a number of different considerations, and the officials are not yet in a position to make any recommendation as to what the attitude of Canada should be. But it is a very hopeful sign, as the Leader of the Opposition points out, that the United States is apparenly planning to move for the strengthening of the jurisdiction of the international court and we shall certainly go into the whole question very carefully. If there is some change that can be made which will strengthen the court and help dispose of some of these disputes, the Canadian government would certainly be in favour of such a change.

I do not rise again to provoke further comment by the minister. It is apparent that the administration is giving consideration to this matter which has been further emphasized by the observations of the Leader of the Opposition. But I do feel so keenly about this particular question and the court generally that I beg leave to say one or two words more.
I am sure that in the processes which are evolving toward the building of international organization it will be recognized that the judicial process is an important one. But if the court has fallen short of expectations, as the minister has just indicated, I think there are reasons other than those he has enumerated. I regret, as one who has followed the procedure of the court both as presently constituted and as it was under the covenant, that I must say that while Canada has been careful in the nominations she has made to the court, that cannot be said for

all other countries. Canada, of course, had a nominee of her own on that court for nine years in the person of Mr. Justice John Reid, formerly head of the legal division in the Department of External Affairs. There have been some great jurists on the court, men such as Sir Arnold McNair and Professor Basdevant. Obviously I am not going to name individuals but anyone who has followed these matters knows perfectly well what I am talking about.
If the court has not been seized with more cases-the minister has mentioned 30 in all and 10 advisory opinions-the reason for it is that a number of decisions of the court -and this is certainly not an overstatement -have had more of a political than a judicial character. The fact that there have been only 10 advisory opinions in a period of 10 years compared with the number of advisory opinions of the older court is an indication that what I am saying is apparently at least worthy of examination.
It may be that at first glance the argument I am now putting forward is an argument against too active consideration at this time of the removal of the compulsory jurisdiction clause. I do not believe that is the case because the removal will not take place forthwith. If we could give some leadership along the lines we have suggested, that together with further emphasis on the desirability of a high calibre of members on the court, will I think strengthen that body. It is noteworthy that students of international law complain bitterly along the lines I have indicated in these few words.
There is one further observation I should like to make on another matter altogether which comes under this item and that is that in the likelihood of a summit meeting or a series of summit meetings, meetings which possibly will be outside the United Nations as such, there is a strong argument for these meetings possibly taking place at the United Nations. Anything that gives additional authority and prestige to the United Nations is, I think, desirable. The meetings in 1954 arising out of the Geneva conference did take place in Geneva at the United Nations building. I simply express the hope, that now that Canada must become reconciled to the fact that the Prime Minister's invitation for the holding of the summit meeting in Canada will not bear fruit, it might be desirable for the minister to give consideration as to what steps Canada could take toward clothing the United Nations with this additional prestige. "Prestige" is hardly the word because the United Nations itself has acquired prestige by its great accomplishments. While all matters having to do with threats to the

peace or with the maintenance of the peace need not necessarily be dealt with under the direct aegis of the United Nations, it seems to me that as much as possible matters of international concern should find a place for discussion within the precincts of the United Nations either in Europe or New York.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few observations I should like to make on the United Nations aspect of this vote. Perhaps I might add to what my colleague the hon. member for Essex East has just said in support of bringing the United Nations into the summit conference to the maximum possible extent. I know the difficulties on that score but I hope they can be overcome and I hope that the secretary general of the United Nations himself could be associated in some way with a summit conference of that kind.
As the minister said in his statement this afternoon this kind of conference is desirable. Perhaps it would have been a good thing if we could have held it a year ago. We would not have had so much talk about it now. I believe it was Earl Atlee who said the other day that he was all for conferences -on the summit, on the slopes, or even on the level-and perhaps they are not always any easier on the level than they are at the summit.
Mention was also made this afternoon of the possible relationship of the United Nations to the Berlin difficulty. That difficulty will again be on the agenda next week at Geneva. The minister said this afternoon there are western rights in Berlin which must be protected. We all agree with that, but the problem is how are these rights going to be protected without causing trouble? How are they going to be maintained in the circumstances in which we find ourselves provided that those who are anxious to weaken or destroy them take steps to that end? And while the United Nations has no direct relationship to this particular problem, and while the secretary general as one would expect has been extremely cautious in any observations he has made-I think confining those observations to the willingness of the United Nations to take any action that is required of it as a result of a four-power
Supply-External Affairs agreement-it may well be that in some form or other, if a deadlock is reached the United Nations will have to be brought in, perhaps through the secretary general again who is a great international trouble shooter, in a form which will make it possible to resolve that dilemma.
There are one or two other United Nations matters which the minister talked about this afternoon. He mentioned the progress that had been made at the Geneva conference in regard to nuclear tests. I confess that that progress has not really been very encouraging though perhaps if there is any progress at all we should take some encouragement from it. The minister expressed the hope that the technical findings which had been agreed upon there might facilitate political agreement. It is not perhaps a matter now for technical findings but for political agreement. I am not sure whether technical agreement, important as it may be, will facilitate political agreement unless there is a will to agree and if there is not a will to agree on this particular problem of nuclear tests, how can we take much hope out of other negotiations for broader progress in disarmament?
The minister mentioned, I think, that 17 articles of a draft treaty had been agreed upon. He knows what the 17 articles are. Most of them, I should think, are the articles that matter least. That would be the normal course of things. There are articles you agree on first and you reserve the difficult ones for later discussion.
This leads me to the subject of disarmament generally which is also in a rather discouraging situation at the United Nations because as a result of all the talk and all the negotiations and all the efforts of the last 10 years we have now reached the position where the agency for further progress is a committee of 83 members of the United Nations. One would have to be very optimistic indeed to get much comfort out of that alteration from a small committee to one of 83 members.
It seems to me that the situation which has resulted in the constitution of this committee of the whole-because that of course is what it is-is one that we should do our best to avoid in the future. The minister knows that the difficulty has been over the kind of balanced representation which the communist bloc at the United Nations will accept and which will also be acceptable to the United States and the western delegations.
There has been a strong effort made by certain of the delegations on the western side in the United Nations to make sure that all the representations should be on a kind of proportionate mathematical basis as a result of which there would always be a predominant majority of non-communist powers. That,

Supply-External Affairs of course, is perfectly reasonable in terms of mathematical representation at the United Nations. But it has resulted in a disarmament committee of 83, and it has also resulted in an outer space committee on which the Russians and their friends will not sit-and indeed where the Indians, as the minister pointed out, will not sit-because the communist delegations have felt they were not given adequate representation. Surely, it is more important at this stage to get general participation in this effort than to worry too much about the exact mathematical proportions of representation on all sides. I throw out the idea to the minister for consideration, whether in the future it might not be a reasonable position for a delegation to adopt, including the Canadian delegation, in order to avoid this kind of deadlock.
The reasonable position is that in principle representations on these United Nations committees, which have a definite political significance, as so many of them have, should be divided, one-third, one-third, one-third- one-third from the western side, one-third from the communist side and one-third from the uncommitted side. There will be very strong objection levelled at that kind of proposal from certain delegations at the United Nations and it does not reflect, I realize, the feelings of the membership of the assembly at the present time, but it is a very reasonable reflection of the division of the world into three camps, the uncommitted camp, the communist camp and what we call occasionally a little loosely the free world. Perhaps the time has come when it is more important to accept that kind of agreed representation in numbers than to set up a committee, one so important as a committee on outer space, which is now working and working very effectively within the limits imposed on it by non-participation of the Indian and the communist states. Perhaps it is more important to get those states participating than to insist on that absolute mathematical proportion of membership which we found so desirable in the past to insist upon. I do not know whether the minister would like to say something about these points before I go on to another matter.

The minister also mentioned this morning something about a permanent stand-by force at the United Nations, a matter which was on the agenda of the United Nations assembly last year, as he pointed out, because of a report of the secretary general. This is a matter on which no progress was possible then for reasons which I think were mentioned in some detail last April when we discussed this matter.


The minister has pointed out an objection to pursuing this question at the present time. In that connection he mentioned that the secretary general himself, who has had a great deal to do with this, of course, has expressed some doubt as to the practicability and the desirability of pushing this issue of a permanent United Nations police or peace force, or stand-by force, whatever you want to call it, at this particular time. The argument that has been advanced not only by the secretary general but by others is that the circumstances which might arise might be of such a character that it would not be possible to organize and constitute a permanent force which would be suitable for all those different situations.
I do not think myself, Mr. Chairman, that that is a very impressive argument. I am not thinking of a United Nations permanent stand-by force which would be trained to meet every emergency which might arise but I am thinking of a United Nations permanent stand-by force which would be on the job ready to go into action if a situation arose which would require that kind of intervention. I have often asked myself in the last year or so what might have happened if we had had that kind of permanently organized and trained and equipped United Nations peace force at the time of the Hungarian uprising. If action could have been taken at the United Nations assembly at that time by a two-thirds majority of the assembly-and I think it would have been possible to get that two-thirds majority- which would have resulted in sending to Hungary a couple of thousand or 1,500 men who would have represented the United Nations as an international force which had been dropped there, if they had gone there, it would have been infinitely more difficult, I think, for any invader or aggressor from the outside to ride roughshod over the freedom fighters in Budapest.
I hope it will be possible in the future to organize and have ready that kind of contingent, ready for action in the various nations which subscribe to the force which could be called upon because they would have made their contingent available in advance. I hope it will soon be possible to have that kind of contingent in being.
When the secretary general put forward the objections which he did, as I understand them-there is a far greater objection, of course, which he has not mentioned because he is a servant of the United Nations and the United Nations consists of 83 members- perhaps the basic objection is that from the communist powers, who insist that this kind of thing would become the agency of what they call the imperialist powers. That is the

reason why when this proposal was made at the last assembly and put forward by the United States it got such a very cold reception in certain quarters and that is why a country like Canada, middle powers like Canada, can take the initiatives in this field which are not open to the big powers. I have already made the suggestion that if it is not practical at the present time to make progress of this kind at the assembly, and it may not be because I know of the difficulties-no one wants to break up the United Nations because of division over this kind of thing-if it is not possible in this way perhaps it would be possible for certain middle powers, six, seven, eight, nine or ten of the status and stature and reputation of Canada to get together and see whether they could not work out some agreement by which they would themselves, through an international agreement binding only on themselves, equip and train certain contingents for international service which would be available to the United Nations if a United Nations assembly resolution was ever passed to call on them for that service. That is the kind of initiative, perhaps, that Canada could take, Mr. Chairman.

It would be a para-military force, I think, a police force which would not have heavy equipment, or anything like that, because this kind of force would be of no use whatever if any country wishes to declare war, or go to war openly against any other country. It would only be of value, -but I think it would be of great value- in policing armistice arrangements, in patrolling disturbed areas such as they are doing now in the Middle East. They could symbolize the United Nations presence when a government of the United Nations wishes to have some kind of United Nations presence on its territory. For instance, when the king of Transjordan thought himself in great danger a year or so ago he considered it a help to have a United Nations presence there on the spot, and they are still there; and it might well be that some one country finding itself threatened could ask for this kind of United Nations intervention. Whether the men would be armed or not perhaps is not so important. They certainly would have side arms; they are not likely to have anything else but they would be there available on the spot. They would be serving under the blue flag of the United Nations. They would represent the international conscience and by their very presence in a disturbed area they might hinder an aggressor's intention. If however an aggressor did decide to move, well, the die would be cast and the United Nations could 66968-9-365

While it may be difficult to make much progress in this matter at the present time,
I think this is an objective which is worth pursuing and I think it is one that perhaps the Canadian government can pursue as effectively as any other member of the United Nations.

Mr. Chairman, very briefly I want to say that the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition are constructive remarks to which the new Secretary of State for External Affairs should give very serious consideration. I think Canada's position in international affairs has been growing in prestige over the years and, with the exception of some recent temporary setbacks, Canada's influence has been growing. If I can judge the mood of the Canadian people they are far more inclined to support action by the United Nations and by a police force than they are action even by such a group of powers as the NATO alliance. Therefore I think this is an opportunity for Canada to give leadership to the world.
We should not only say to the United Nations and campaign in the United Nations for the creation of a permanent police force to which Canada would make a substantial contribution but I think we should go even further. Although this further step might be considered only a gesture, although it might be considered rather impractical at this time, I think it would create a real impact in the world if a middle power such as Canada, a power that is identified with the west, a power that shares the northern regions with the Soviet union, were to announce by way of a national policy that Canada was prepared to place all of her troops and armed forces at the disposal of the United Nations for such a police force.
I am hopeful that the day will arrive when national armaments can be cut back, indeed that the day will arrive when nothing more than a national police force will be necessary and that national armed forces and national defence as we now know it may become a thing of the past. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, such an Atlantic Nations police force could not withstand a nuclear attack or attack by a major power. It seems to me that in this day and age defence against nuclear attack is becoming more and more difficult. That being the case, an international police force comprising defence forces having at their disposal in the main or perhaps exclusively conventional weapons is an important need to protect the world against brush fire attacks, as they are called, and is also important as a gesture to all the nations

I view with great misgiving any decision by the Canadian government to permit nuclear and thermonuclear weapons within Canada, and I think this kind of gesture by Canada, this kind of idea advanced by the new Secretary of State for External Affairs would be the type of bold and imaginative action that might receive far more support at this time than we might expect. Mr. Chairman, the United Nations special fund, the establishment of which was decided by the twelfth general assembly, will begin operations in 1959. The new fund is designed to assist projects in the fields of resource surveys, technical training, demonstrations, education, public administration, etc. The fund will concentrate on relatively large projects so as to avoid undue dispersion of its resources. It will be controlled by a governing council which will consist of 18 states elected from members of the United Nations and its specialized agencies and will provide for equal representation of economically more developed countries and underdeveloped countries. Provision has been made for a close working association with the international bank.
The United States is prepared to give up to $38 million to ETAP and the special fund taken together, on condition that the United States contribution is not more than 40 per cent of the total pledged to both programs. United Kingdom authorities have in mind a contribution to the fund equal to approximately 7 per cent of the fund's total resources, that is, $2.24 million if total contributions amount to $30 million. The Netherlands are pledged to make a contribution of $2.4 million, while the contributions of France and the Soviet union will be of the order of $1 million each. Italy has pledged $1 million to be divided between ETAP and the special fund. Japan has pledged $480,000 to the special fund. Some of the pledges contain matching provisions. Cabinet decided on September 30 that, subject to the approval of parliament, Canada will contribute $2 million U.S. to the special fund in 1959-60.

Vote 90 deals with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and perhaps this provides an opportunity for me to say a word about the organization and perhaps ask the minister a question or two. There is no need for anyone in this committee to elaborate on the importance of this organization, both in a military and nonmilitary way. The minister told us about that this afternoon. But I think that anyone who appreciates, as we all do, the importance of NATO and who reflects on what might have happened to the western world if NATO had not been founded 10 years ago, must worry about some of the developments that are now taking place which, on the face of them, and with the information that is available to those who have not other sources of information, seem to threaten the vitality and development of the organization.
There is bound to be, of course, difficulty in the development of an organization of this kind. Perhaps we get a little too impatient and we think that in 10 years we should do that which has not been done in hundreds or thousands of years before, the building up of a collective organization not only for security but for nonmilitary purposes. In the context of history, we have undoubtedly made progress but I worry, as I am sure other hon. members worry, that we may lose some of that progress. If we do not move forward in NATO, we are not going to stand still and undoubtedly we will move backward.
Some of these things that worry us have come to a head, for instance, as illustrated in the decision made yesterday and which was announced in the house today, of the withdrawal of United States NATO squadrons, on orders of the NATO commander, from the NATO airfields in France to airfields out of France because of a dispute between France and the United States over the control and possession of nuclear weapons to be used in an emergency by those squadrons or to be used perhaps from those air bases in the form of missiles. I should like to think of that kind of consultation developing in NATO, because if it does not, then as a political agency NATO will weaken and as the atmosphere of crisis disappears, NATO will disappear with it.

Finally, there is the question of economic co-operation, not inside NATO itself because NATO perhaps is not the right agency to act for its members in respect of economic questions. However, if economic matters develop in Europe in such a way that we have two European economic groups and a North American economic group, and economic conflict develops between those groups, or if nonco-operation develops between those groups, then NATO as a political and military agency is going to feel the effect of that development. It will weaken the organization.
Those are the three main dangers, as I see them, which confront this essential collective security organization at the present time. There is the military threat because of the tendency now to split apart rather than to come together, and look after our own defences. This tendency was also illustrated a few months ago when the French government felt it necessary to take part of its Mediterranean fleet out of NATO control. I do not criticize the French for that because the major part of the British fleet and the major part of the United States fleet are not under NATO control.
If we criticize the French for that, we should remember that the whole question of our continental defence was taken out of NATO control or, indeed, was never under NATO control. The French probably thought of that when they began to make their own adjustments in the Mediterranean. So there is this military danger to collective action, there is the political danger of nonco-operation and then there is the economic danger of conflict between the two European economic areas which may be developing and a North American economic area which may be separating from Europe. I do not know whether it is asking too much to ask the minister at this time to say something about this matter but I will do so just the same.

I see no sign of the disintegration of NATO. "We all understand that if there were to be such a disintegration it would be disastrous

It is true that from time to time difficult problems arise, and the one raised by the Leader of the Opposition on the orders of the day this morning is a difficult one. However, I do not consider that it would be of much help in the solution of this difficult problem for me as the foreign minister of Canada or, for that matter, for the other foreign ministers to start placing blame or being critical. In these questions I have found that there are always two sides, and sometimes more. Of course, that statement applies to domestic issues as well as to issues in the foreign field. However, I can assure the Leader of the Opposition that this government has done and will continue to do everything possible to assist in getting these problems ironed out. As hon. members know, we even have problems in Canada between ten provinces. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is an expert on problems of this sort. Wherever there are human beings trying to work along together, I suppose there are bound to be problems.
With regard also to co-operation in the economic field, I think there is no reason for discouragement. Two or three weeks ago we had a visit from the presidents of the three European communities. To me it was quite startling to realize to what extent these six European nations had been able to work out methods of co-operation, especially the French and the Germans. I found it almost beyond comprehension when I learned of the extent to which they have gone in working out methods for co-operation. We have had reports here this afternoon from two of the members of the house who attended the Atlantic congress. They have reported that the meetings of this conference were highly successful and that is the opinion of the government. The whole trend is toward more co-operation.

I noticed also the minister said something at an earlier stage, if I remember correctly when he made an announcement the other day on orders of the day, about sounding out provincial governments concerning the possibility [DOT]of taking some of these refugees who could not satisfy immigration regulations on the grounds of health, particularly those people who were tubercular. The minister may or may not know, but the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration certainly would know, that in the case of the Hungarian refugees whom we took in in considerable numbers who could
not satisfy immigration health regulations, the federal government undertook, and I believe is still carrying out the undertaking, to look after whatever medical care was necessary. I should like to express the view that if you expect the provincial governments to undertake this as a provincial charge, we will get absolutely nowhere. It is not unreasonable that the provinces should take that view, and for this reason: We want people who come to live in Canada to be mobile and able to move freely from one province to another. It is, therefore, not reasonable to expect the provincial governments to provide these facilities free. I am sure most provinces would provide them at cost, or at a very reasonable rate.
I think if we are serious about doing something about this problem, and I hope we are, the federal government will have to undertake to reimburse the provinces for their out-ofpocket costs in connection with the matter.

I regard this as an important vote. We have, under vote 100, talked about assistance for some two million refugees, other than those who come under the operations of the United Nations relief and works agency for Palestine refugees in the Near East. It is about the latter that I wish to say something. There are some one million of these refugees, and as I had the opportunity last September of visiting three of the camps where hundreds of thousands of these refugees are to be found in the Gaza strip and in Jordan, I believe we ought to have this matter projected for the consideration of the government in terms of a definitive solution.
This problem of one million people is now almost 10 years old. It is one of the most difficult problems of its kind in the field of current international responsibilities. The matter is one now that has risen beyond the capacity of the country from which most of these refugees have come. Whatever may be the moral obligation of Israel, the problem now has assumed proportions that give it a true international character. I would say that the work of this agency, in terms of providing maintenance, shelter and food is not wanting, but there remains bitterness and dissatisfaction on the part of these refugees whose numbers are increasing by natural growth. Unless the problem is met with some resoluteness, not by one nation or by two nations in the Middle East but by all of the nations, we are allowing to evolve a problem that may increasingly add to the troubles of that turbulent area.

Now, as I understand it, the work of this agency is to be reviewed or terminated in 1960. I would be interested in knowing what the view of the government is with regard to the continued operations of this organization. What steps are being taken by Canada as a member of the United Nations to seek to resolve the problem in some way. It cannot be allowed to continue in its present state without creating complicated problems for the future. I wonder if the minister could tell us if he has had an opportunity yet of reviewing this situation, and what he thinks government policy in Canada should be? How long should we continue to provide financial assistance, and to what extent are we prepared to play our part in bringing some solution to this very difficult problem, one that is involving day by day great human tragedy. This is a question to which a country like Canada should address itself with forthrightness and with a resolution to seek a solution of the problem. I ask the minister if he would care to comment on what I have said.

No. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate raised a number of questions concerning our procurements in the Atlantic provinces. First, he asked for the dollar increase in 1958-59 for all defence

purchases in the Atlantic provinces. As I reported on June 3, head office purchases from Atlantic province firms last year amounted to $21.8 million, and district office purchases for this area-the vast majority of which were from local firms-were over $15 million. These give a combined total of $37 million as against $30 million in the previous year.
I must qualify this-as I did before-in several ways. First, as I have indicated, the district office purchases include a small percentage of orders placed with firms outside the area, but our records do not give precise information on this point. Second, the figures do not include defence subcontracts within the area

which excludes, for example, the work being done by Enamel and Heating Products on the CS2F program. Third, as the hon. member for Ottawa West observed on Wednesday, the addresses on contracts- which provide the basis of our regional breakdown-often do not show the actual site of production. For example, many of our purchases of Nova Scotia coal are made from firms with a Quebec or Ontario address and are not, for this reason, included in the figures I have given.
Second, the member asked what proportion of the increase was on construction, what on ship building and ship repairing, and what on procurement of an industrial character. Construction figures, of course, have been excluded from the amounts I reported for purchasing. In 1958-1959 construction orders, including a small amount of maintenance, amounted to $20 million. In the previous year, the corresponding figure was only $6 million, and it is because I did not feel that this offered a fair comparison that I did not include these figures in my June 3 statement.
Ship building and ship repairing orders in the Atlantic provinces last year were $12.5 million, and in the previous year $8.5 million. The increase is therefore $4 million, which represents 57 per cent of the total increase in purchases.
Unfortunately, I am unable to say anything about procurement of an industrial character. However, it may be of assistance to the hon. member if I give as much of a breakdown as our records permit.
One category, aircraft components and overhaul, which is readily shown by our records, accounted for $5.1 million last year and $3.8 million the year before; giving an increase of $1.3 million which is 18 per cent of the total increase. Coal purchases directly from Atlantic provinces dealers actually show a decline from $2.4 million to $2.2 million, although there was, in fact, a substantial increase in our total purchases of maritime
Supply-Defence Production coal over the period, which does not show up because the actual contracts were, in many cases, placed with firms in central Canada.
This, then, leaves only a residual amount of $2 million for 1958-59 and $1.7 million for the previous year, excluding district office purchases. Presumably the figures wanted by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate representing purchases of an industrial character, lie within these totals, together with a portion of the amounts I reported for aircraft parts and overhaul.
The last part of the hon. member's question had to do with a distinction between projects initiated by the present government and those started by the previous administration. I regret that I have no figures to answer this, and I would point out to the hon. member that he has, in fact, directed his question to the wrong source. As he knows, my department and Defence Construction Limited do not initiate any projects-we simply contract for the supply or construction of the goods, services and defence works which are requisitioned by the Department of National Defence. I might repeat, however, what I said on June 3, that within my own sphere of responsibility, as the minister charged with procurement, I have sought to improve the Atlantic provinces' share of defence contract expenditures. I believe that the figures show that we have made progress in this direction, and I would assure the hon. member that we shall continue our efforts.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SIGNING OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: The Municipal Grants Act does not specifically cover these plants but provides for taxes on federal property to be paid in full subject to adjustment with respect to services rendered.
